# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel (2026-11-20)

## Short version

The jf2 memory allocator lowered the 99th-percentile latency of the kestrel key-value store from 2140 to 870 microseconds. Throughput and median latency showed no measurable change in this read-heavy test. The 5.7 GB (9.3%) rise in memory use still needs approval from the capacity team.

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: our key-value store.
- **jemalloc**: the memory allocator that kestrel uses today, at version 5.3.
- **jf2**: our fork of jemalloc.
- **YCSB**: Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark, a standard benchmark for key-value stores.
- **ycsb-b**: the read-heavy YCSB workload (95% reads, 5% updates by default) [Ref4].
- **ycsb-a**: the write-heavy YCSB workload (50% reads, 50% updates by default) [Ref4].
- **p50**: the median latency. Half of the requests finish faster.
- **p99, p99.9**: 99% and 99.9% of requests finish faster than these values.
- **Tail latency**: the latency of the slowest requests, here p99 and p99.9.
- **Latency spike**: a short period with much higher latency than normal.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **kops/s**: thousands of operations per second.
- **RSS**: resident set size (the physical memory the process holds).
- **Decay purge**: jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay.
- **perf**: the Linux profiling tool.
- **je_arena_decay**: a jemalloc function in the decay purge code.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding a process to the CPUs and memory of one processor socket.
- **Staging**: the pre-production environment.

## Goal

Check whether jf2 removes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.

## Test setup

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Host | bench-07 (the test server) |
| CPUs | 2 x 32-core Xeon |
| Memory | 512 GB |
| Kernel | Linux 6.8 |
| Load average before the runs | 0.4 on 64 cores (the host was almost idle) |
| Build A | main at commit 4f1c2aa, jemalloc 5.3 |
| Build B | main at commit 4f1c2aa, jf2 |
| Workload | ycsb-b, 64 client threads |
| Runs | 5 per build, 10 minutes each |
| Order | alternating: A, B, A, B, ... |

## Results

```
Latency in us, median of 5 runs.
One block = 200 us. Shorter is better.

p50    A | 118
       B | 119      no measurable change

p99    A ███████████ 2140
       B ████ 870      59% lower

p99.9  A █████████████████████████████████████████████████ 9800
       B ████████████████ 3100      68% lower
```

Only p99 and p99.9 changed. p50 and throughput showed no measurable change.

Each cell shows the median of 5 runs, then the lowest and highest run. No range was recorded for RSS.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change in median |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput (kops/s) | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -0.7% |
| p50 latency (us) | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +0.8% |
| p99 latency (us) | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -59% |
| p99.9 latency (us) | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -68% |
| RSS at end of run (GB) | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 GB (+9.3%) |

## What the data shows

- **Tail latency**: build B is lower. The median p99 fell by 59%. The median p99.9 fell by 68% [Ref1].
- **Run-to-run check**: the ranges of A and B do not overlap for p99 or p99.9 [Ref1].
  - For p99, the highest B run (940 us) is below the lowest A run (1890 us).
  - For p99.9, the highest B run (3900 us) is below the lowest A run (7200 us).
- **Throughput**: the medians differ by 3 kops/s (0.7%). The run ranges of A and B overlap [Ref1]. So the test shows no measurable difference.
- **Median latency**: the medians differ by 1 us (0.8%). The run ranges overlap [Ref1]. So the test shows no measurable difference.
- **Memory**: RSS at the end of the run is 5.7 GB (9.3%) higher in build B [Ref1].

## Cause of the spikes in build A

- **Observation**: the spikes in build A occur at the same time as the jemalloc decay purge. In the spike windows, 31% of the perf samples are in je_arena_decay [Ref2].
- **Difference in build B**: jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.
- **Hypothesis**: the background purge is the reason for the lower tail latency. A perf profile of build B during its slowest periods would confirm or reject this.

## Deviation from the plan

1. Run 3 of build B stalled for 40 s at minute 7.
2. We traced the stall to logrotate (a log archiving tool). The nightly cron job (a scheduled system task) started it. The allocator was not the cause [Ref3].
3. We repeated the run. The B results use the repeated run in place of the stalled run.

## Not tested

- ycsb-a
- more than 64 client threads
- NUMA pinning

So the result holds only for the read-heavy workload at 64 client threads.

## Open question

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must approve it.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a on 2026-11-21.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If the capacity team approves, enable jf2 in staging. A feature flag (an on/off switch in the configuration) will control it.

## References

- [Ref1] Results table in this report. Data: 5 runs per build on bench-07, 2026-11-20.
- [Ref2] perf profile of build A, sampled in the spike windows, 2026-11-20.
- [Ref3] Investigation of the 40 s stall in run 3 of build B, 2026-11-20.
- [Ref4] YCSB wiki, "Core Workloads" page: github.com/brianfrankcooper/YCSB/wiki/Core-Workloads

---

Things I added that are not in your notes. Check them before you send the report.

- **Computed values**: the percent changes and the range-overlap statements come from your medians and min..max values.
- **Hypothesis label**: your notes hold a perf profile of build A only. If you also profiled build B, replace the hypothesis with that data.
- **Workload mix**: the read and update percentages are the YCSB defaults. Change them if your configuration differs.
- **Step 3 condition**: I read "if ok" as the capacity team's approval only. Add the ycsb-a result as a second condition if you meant both.
- **References**: they name the data but hold no paths. Add links to the raw run logs if the team needs them.
